title: Choosing tomato varieties
subtitle: What to grow for flavour, reliability, and the UK growing season
excerpt: With hundreds of tomato varieties available, choosing comes down to three factors: type (cordon or bush), growing location (greenhouse or outdoor), and the UK season length. This guide covers the most reliable choices for flavour and productivity in a British garden.
sourceNotes: RHS tomato variety guide (rhs.org.uk). USDA cooperative extension notes on tomato variety selection, public domain. Historical variety records from RHS AGM award lists, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: An indeterminate tomato variety trained as a single upright stem by removing all side shoots (pinching out). Cordon tomatoes are tied to a cane or string as they grow. They continue growing until the tip is removed, often reaching 1.5 to 2 m. Most traditional large-fruited varieties are cordons. They produce fewer but larger fruits over a longer period than bush types.

A determinate tomato variety that reaches a fixed height, produces all its fruit over a shorter period, and needs no side-shooting. Bush types are better for outdoor growing in the UK, where the shorter season suits their compact, concentrated cropping habit. Tumbling Tom, Tornado, and Tumbler are compact bush types suitable for containers and growing bags.

content.text: The most important choice is between
types. Cordons need regular side-shooting and support; they crop over a longer period. Bush types need no pruning and suit the shorter outdoor UK season.

Under cover, cordon varieties thrive in the extended warmth and give high yields. Alicante and Shirley are reliable for greenhouse growing, with good resistance to greenback (a hard green patch on the shoulder). Sungold is a widely-grown orange cherry tomato with exceptional flavour. Gardener's Delight is a red cherry variety with high disease resistance and a long harvest period. Marmande and San Marzano are large meaty types suited to sauce-making.

Outdoor growing suits early, blight-tolerant types. Tumbling Tom (bush, red or yellow) is good in pots and hanging baskets. Tornado and Red Alert are reliable bush types for borders. Ferline and Legend are both cordon varieties with useful blight tolerance.

Avoid large beefsteak varieties outdoors; they need more warmth than most UK summers provide. Varieties bred for hot, sunny climates will fruit but often taste thin and bland in a cool season. Look for Award of Garden Merit (AGM) varieties when choosing outdoor types; AGM testing for tomatoes uses UK conditions.
